name: Record Atlas surname families
note: Which spellings are one name, and what each claim rests on. The only catalogue of surname variants in this project: the family archives do not keep their own. A form is listed once; case, accents, spaces, apostrophes and a spaced particle (Defranceschi, De Franceschi) are one form and are derived, not stored. Surname strings, places, periods and kinds of record only: no given name and no identifier. Written with scripts/surname_variants.py; read by the surname pages and by every session.

statuses.same: One record, or the family's own tree, writes one person or family both ways.
statuses.attested: Met on a record of this family's line by the archive that read it.
statuses.rule: Reached by a documented mechanical substitution. No record needed.
statuses.lead: Plausible and never seen on a record. Search it; never write a data row on it alone.
statuses.case-by-case: Sometimes this family, sometimes another. Decide per record.
statuses.not-same: A different name that turns up in searches. Recorded so it is not decided twice.

rules.diacritic-fold: The index folds the mark: a search for one returns the other's records.
rules.translit: A documented substitution when a Slavic name crosses a Latin-alphabet border (ć written ch, š sh).
rules.ending: A systematic ending change between languages (-schi / -ski, -ić / -ich).

families.name: Lerena
families.note: Rio de la Plata and Extremadura. A clerk's L, S, G, P or tilde is the commonest reason a search for Lerena finds nothing.

evidence.what: The ordinary form in the Rio de la Plata and the spelling the family archive uses as its own (135 rows).
An 1889 Buenos Aires probate writes one man both Lerena and Llerena, twice each, in one hand. Also the commoner form in Spain, from the Extremaduran town.
The parish registers of one Uruguayan city spell one man's name both ways across forty years.
An 1811 baptism names a grandparent Gerena in the same sentence that writes the father Llerena.
Written by the priest himself on a marriage act of 1825, and on a Montevideo cathedral act of 1879. Not a transcriber's error.
The transcript of the 1858 Trinidad diagram reads Leresa where the plate says Lerena. A transcript's spelling, not the clerk's.
An original act of October 1833 names a family Lerina. The archive had excluded the form as Italian and took that back.
A godparent on the same 1879 Montevideo act that writes the father Lereña and the grandfather Serena: four spellings of one family's name on one page.
The 1858 Trinidad kinship diagram writes family members Lorena, and the family's central army enrolment record was indexed under it.
An 1879 Montevideo cathedral act and a Trinidad kinship diagram of 1858 write the family's name Serena. A sweep on it found children for two couples the archive had worked for weeks.
Ten hits in the Uruguay census collection 1726-1858, two of them complete households.
FamilySearch folds the n-tilde: a search for Sereña returns the identical 290 records as Serena. No separate sweep is needed.
Listed beside Lereña as the tilde-added form; no record of its own is cited.
Fourteen people under this form in Santa Fe and Entre Rios, 1837-1913. At Cayasta it is an Italian colony's name and not this family; in Entre Rios it shadows the Lerena family.
A father's surname on an 1899 marriage, and the same man written Serena in the companion volume. Perena is also a surname in its own right: a lead, not a relative, until an act says otherwise.
